$comment: Mutation definitions for spec 009 (in-page autofill overlay).
This file is the mutation table. It used to live in PR bodies, where it
drifted twice: a stale kill count in #37, and a Slice A2 row (A2-M4,
registration-id injectivity) that survived with ZERO kills for a full slice
because the property was asserted only in a code comment.
Each mutation names a security property, the literal edits that break it,
and the number of tests that must die. `expectedKills` is measured, never
guessed: run the runner, read the number, pin it here. A drifted number is
reported as a failure, which is the whole point of committing this file.
`find` is matched as a LITERAL string, never a regex, and must match exactly
`expect` times (default 1). A definition that matches nothing is a hard
error, not a silent pass.
WHY THESE NUMBERS DIFFER FROM THE PR BODIES
If you are comparing this file against the tables in PR #40, #47 or #50 and
the numbers disagree: THIS FILE IS THE REFERENCE. The tables are snapshots
of a suite that no longer exists. Three known, deliberate divergences:
* EVERY A0 ROW. PR #40 measured against a 100-test Node suite. Slice A2
grew it to 179 (content_overlay behavioural tests via fake_page.js, and
the crash-injection cases), and closing the A2-M7 survivor made it 180.
The A0 mutations were not weakened and the A0 policy did not change —
there are simply more tests in the blast radius. A0 counts going UP
against #40 is expected; going DOWN is a regression worth chasing.
* A2-M4. PR #50 recorded '4 kills'. That was a UNIT ERROR: 4 assertions
inside ONE test case. This runner counts test cases, so 1 is correct.
See the row's own comment.
* A1-M2. PR #47 recorded 14, this file measures 10, because the mutation
here is a tighter reconstruction and the Flutter suite is targeted at
four files. See the row's own comment.
The general rule: a number in a PR body was true once and is now unowned;
a number in this file is re-measured on every run and fails the build when
it drifts. Do not 'correct' this file to match a PR — re-run the runner.

slices.A0: security harness for the overlay (overlay_security.js) — PR #40
slices.A1: native exact-origin contract for the reveal path — PR #47
slices.A2: per-origin opt-in with crash-consistent revocation — PR #50

not wrong so much as measuring something else, for two reasons:
1. This mutation is a TIGHTER reconstruction of 'put the domain branch
back'. It re-admits a domain identifier only when the value equals the

mutations.property: two distinct permission patterns can never collide onto one registration id, which would silently unregister a still-authorized site
$comment: THIS IS THE ROW THAT SURVIVED A FULL SLICE WITH ZERO KILLS. The property
was claimed only in the comment above registrationIdForPattern. A
modulo-16 encoding merges same-length hosts whose code points differ by
exactly 16 (a/q, b/r). If this ever returns to 0, the guard is gone.
UNIT CORRECTION: the hand-written table recorded '4 kills' for this row.
That was never 4 TEST CASES — only one test asserts injectivity
('A018: the registration id is injective, including on lossy-encoding
twins'), and no lossy variant tried (modulo-16, last-digit truncation,
sum-hash) kills more than that one test. The 4 counted assertions or twin
pairs inside that single test. This runner counts test cases, so the
measured value is 1. The property is held; the unit was wrong.

mutations.title: reconcile no longer clears in-memory grants
mutations.property: a reconciliation triggered by a permission change drops every focus grant
$comment: CLOSED. Found as a SURVIVOR by this runner on its first full execution,
and closed by the test it demanded.
Third instance of the same failure mode as A2-M4 and the content_overlay
gap: the property is stated in spec.md:296 ('first load/validate durable
config, clear all in-memory grants, then reconcile...') and repeated in a
comment above the call, and NO test asserted it.
Never a live vulnerability: an external revocation also bumps the config
revision, and FocusGrantStore.consume() rejects a grant whose
configRevision is stale. The grant clear is defence in depth — but it was
defence in depth that nothing held, which is how it silently rots.
THE TEST ASSERTS THE EFFECT, NOT THE STATE. The obvious closure — mint a
grant, reconcile, assert `worker.grants.size === 0` — was NOT written.
Inspecting the data structure is the same class of weakness as the three
gaps above: it re-states the implementation instead of the guarantee, and
would go green against any refactor that keeps the Map tidy while leaving
a token redeemable. The test redeems the token through the real
FocusGrantStore.consume() path and requires it to fail.
The setup is what makes the number mean anything: the permission is still
granted and the config is valid, so this reconcile commits nothing and the
revision does not move. That deliberately disarms the downstream
configRevision check — the very thing that made this survivor harmless —
so the ONLY remaining explanation for a rejected consume is the grant
clear. The test pins that with an explicit assertion on the revision, and
redeems a second grant BEFORE the reconcile as a control so it cannot pass
vacuously on a consume that was always going to fail.

mutations.title: registration id hex is unpadded (variable width)
mutations.property: the fixed 4-hex-digit width is what makes the encoding injective for an arbitrary code point
$comment: Found BY the runner while probing A2-M4 variants, not by reading the code.
Unpadded hex survives the A018 injectivity test because every host in that
test is ASCII, and every ASCII code point is exactly 2 hex digits — so the
variable-width encoding is still injective over the tested alphabet.
It is injective over the REACHABLE alphabet too: permission patterns are
built from canonicalized ASCII hosts (IDNA is refused fail-closed in Slice
A1), so a code point above 0xff cannot reach this function.
Recorded as equivalent rather than as a gap: the padding is defence in
depth against an input canonicalization already forbids. If IDNA support
ever lands, that argument dies and this mutation starts killing.
WHERE THE REACHABILITY ARGUMENT IS ENFORCED — check these before
believing this row is still equivalent:
* overlay_security.js, canonicalizeOrigin(): a non-ASCII host is
refused fail-closed, never folded through a mapping table.
* browser_exact_origin.dart: the Dart half refuses the same input, so
neither side can hand a non-ASCII pattern to the other.
* permissionPatternForOrigin() builds the pattern only from an already
canonicalized origin, so this function has no other input path.
This equivalence is therefore CONDITIONAL, and the condition is machine-
checked rather than trusted: `equivalent: true` with `expectedKills: 0`
makes the runner treat ANY kill as drift and fail --check. The day IDNA
lands, this row goes red on its own instead of quietly staying true-by-
accident. Do not delete the row to make that noise stop — the noise is
the feature.
mutations.equivalentReason: Patterns are derived only from canonicalized ASCII hosts, so every code point is 2 hex digits and unpadded hex stays injective. Killing this requires a non-ASCII pattern, which canonicalizeOrigin() (JS) and browser_exact_origin.dart (Dart) both refuse fail-closed. If IDNA support lands, this argument dies and the mutation starts killing, which the runner reports as drift.
